L5@P0: Abstract: We describe linear-time algorithms for solving a class of problems that involve
L6@P0: transforming a cost function on a grid using spatial information. These problems can be
L7@P0: viewed as a generalization of classical distance transforms of binary images, where the
L8@P0: binary image is replaced by an arbitrary function on a grid. Alternatively they can be viewed
L9@P0: in terms of the minimum convolution of two functions, which is an important operation in
L10@P0: grayscale morphology. A consequence of our techniques is a simple and fast method for
L11@P0: computing the Euclidean distance transform of a binary image. Our algorithms are also
L12@P0: applicable to Viterbi decoding, belief propagation, and optimal control.
L13@P0: ACM Classification: F.2.1, I.4
L14@P0: AMS Classification: 68T45, 68W40
L15@P0: Key words and phrases: distance transform, minimum convolution, image processing
L16@P0: 1 Introduction
L17@P0: Distance transforms are an important tool in computer vision, image processing and pattern recognition.
L18@P0: A distance transform of a binary image specifies the distance from each pixel to the nearest “on” pixel.
L19@P0: Distance transforms play a central role in the comparison of binary images, particularly for images
L20@P0: resulting from local feature detection techniques such as edge or corner detection. For example, both
L21@P0: the Chamfer [6] and Hausdorff [16] matching approaches make use of distance transforms in comparing
L22@P0: binary images. Distance transforms are also used to compute the medial axis (boundaries of Voronoi
L23@P0: cells) of digital shapes [4].
L24@P0: In this paper we consider a generalization of distance transforms to arbitrary functions on a grid rather
L25@P0: than binary-valued ones (i. e., real-valued images rather than binary images). There is a simple intuition
L26@P0: underlying this generalization. Binary images are often used to specify the locations of certain features in
L27@P0: a picture. Rather than using a binary array to specify the presence or absence of a feature at each pixel, it

L31@P1: such more general situation it is again useful to compute a type of distance transform, which in this case
L32@P1: should reflect a combination of distances and feature costs.
L33@P1: Let G be a regular grid and f :G→R a function on the grid. We refer to a function on a grid as a
L34@P1: sampled function. Sampled functions are usually defined by arrays. We define the distance transform of f

L67@P1: Efficient algorithms for computing the distance transform of a binary image using the L1 and L∞
L68@P1: distances were developed by Rosenfeld and Pfaltz [27]. Similar methods described in [5] have been
L69@P1: widely used to compute approximations to the EDT of a binary image. These algorithms can be easily
L70@P1: adapted to compute the distance transform of a sampled function, as we show in Section 3 for the case of
L71@P1: the L1 distance.
L72@P1: Our main result is a new linear-time algorithm for computing the distance transform of a sampled
L73@P1: function when distance is measured by the squared Euclidean distance. This in turn provides a new
L74@P1: technique for computing the exact EDT of a binary image, by computing the transform of the corresponding indicator function and taking square roots of the result. There are a number of other algorithms
L75@P1: for computing the EDT of a binary image in linear-time (e. g., [18, 7, 17]); however these methods are
L76@P1: quite involved and are not widely used in practice. In contrast, our algorithm is relatively simple, easy to

L78@P2: implement, and very fast in practice. In the Conclusions (Section 5) we indicate the range of areas of
L79@P2: science and technology to which our algorithm has already been applied.
L80@P2: A sampled function is equivalent to a real-valued image. We use the terminology “distance transform
L81@P2: of a sampled function” for two reasons. First, we want to stress that the input is generally some kind of
L82@P2: cost function that is being transformed so as to incorporate spatial (or distance) information. Second,
L83@P2: there are methods for computing transforms of real-valued images based on minimum distances along
L84@P2: paths, where the cost of a path is the sum of values along the path [28]. We want to avoid confusion with
L85@P2: these methods which compute something quite different from what we consider here.
L86@P2: 1.1 Minimum convolution
L87@P2: The distance transform of a function is closely related to the min-convolution operation. This operation
L88@P2: and its continuous counterpart play an important role in grayscale morphology [21]. The min-convolution
L89@P2: of two functions f and g is defined as,
L90@P2: (f ⊗g)(p) = min
L91@P2: q
L92@P2: 
L93@P2: f(q) +g(p−q)

L96@P2: Just like standard convolution, this operation is commutative and associative,
L97@P2: f ⊗g = g⊗ f,
L98@P2: (f ⊗h)⊗g = f ⊗(h⊗g).
L99@P2: When d(p,q) = g(p−q), the distance transform of f under the distance d is the min-convolution
L100@P2: of f and g. The algorithms we describe in this paper can be seen as a algorithms for computing minconvolutions with restricted functions g. Our basic algorithms solve one-dimensional problems. The
L101@P2: multi-dimensional case is handled by decomposing it into a sequence of one-dimensional problems.
L102@P2: In the case of the squared Euclidean distance we are computing the min-convolution of a onedimensional function f and a parabola. We solve the problem by noting a relationship to lower envelopes
L103@P2: of parabolas. Lower envelopes of n parabolas can be computed in O(nlogn) time using the method in [8].
L104@P2: That method operates by sorting the parabolas in an appropriate order to be inserted in the lower envelope
L105@P2: in amortized constant time. In our case we get an O(n) algorithm because the parabolas have the same
L106@P2: shape and are already sorted in an appropriate order. Here n is the size of the domain of f . In the case of
L107@P2: the L1 distance we compute the min-convolution of a one-dimensional function f and a cone using the
L108@P2: classical approach of Rosenfeld and Pfaltz [27].
L109@P2: When d is the squared Euclidean and L1 distance, the corresponding g is convex. As described by
L110@P2: Eppstein [9] the problem of computing one-dimensional min-convolutions between arbitrary functions f
L111@P2: and convex functions g can be solved in O(n) time using the totally monotone matrix search algorithm
L112@P2: of [1]. When g is concave the problem can be solved in O(nα(n)) time using the matrix search algorithm
L113@P2: of [20], where α is the extremely slowly growing inverse Ackermann function.
L114@P2: Our algorithm for one-dimensional min-convolution with a parabola generalizes to computing the
L115@P2: min-convolution of an arbitrary one-dimensional function f and a convex or concave function g. If an
L116@P2: intersection point between shifted copies of g can be computed in constant time we get an O(n) method
L117@P2: for computing the min-convolution (the resulting algorithm is simpler than the linear-time method based
L118@P2: on matrix search, and also applies to the case when g is concave). Otherwise binary search can be used to
L119@P2: find an intersection in O(logn) time, yielding an O(nlogn) min-convolution algorithm.

L147@P3: 1.3 Classical EDT
L148@P3: An important consequence of our results is a new linear-time algorithm for computing the classical
L149@P3: Euclidean distance transform of a binary image. The method works by decomposing the problem into a
L150@P3: sequence of one-dimensional problems. This decomposition relies on the solution of the more general
L151@P3: problem, involving transforms of sampled functions. Thus, by solving a more general problem for the
L152@P3: one-dimensional case we obtain a simple algorithm for the multi-dimensional EDT.
L153@P3: While other methods for computing the EDT of binary functions existed before, these methods have
L154@P3: not been used in practice due to their practical complexity. In contrast, our algorithm has been used in a
L155@P3: wide variety of applications. For example, it was applied to study urban change in [15], motion planning
L156@P3: in [25], object recognition in [29] and image analysis PDEs in [22]. This illustrates the significance of
L157@P3: developing algorithms that are not only asymptotically optimal, but are also easy to implement and have
L158@P3: low complexity in practice.

L5@P0: Abstract: We describe linear-time algorithms for solving a class of problems that involve
L6@P0: transforming a cost function on a grid using spatial information. These problems can be
L7@P0: viewed as a generalization of classical distance transforms of binary images, where the
L8@P0: binary image is replaced by an arbitrary function on a grid. Alternatively they can be viewed
L9@P0: in terms of the minimum convolution of two functions, which is an important operation in
L10@P0: grayscale morphology. A consequence of our techniques is a simple and fast method for
L11@P0: computing the Euclidean distance transform of a binary image. Our algorithms are also
L12@P0: applicable to Viterbi decoding, belief propagation, and optimal control.

L16@P0: 1 Introduction
L17@P0: Distance transforms are an important tool in computer vision, image processing and pattern recognition.
L18@P0: A distance transform of a binary image specifies the distance from each pixel to the nearest “on” pixel.
L19@P0: Distance transforms play a central role in the comparison of binary images, particularly for images
L20@P0: resulting from local feature detection techniques such as edge or corner detection. For example, both
L21@P0: the Chamfer [6] and Hausdorff [16] matching approaches make use of distance transforms in comparing
L22@P0: binary images. Distance transforms are also used to compute the medial axis (boundaries of Voronoi
L23@P0: cells) of digital shapes [4].
L24@P0: In this paper we consider a generalization of distance transforms to arbitrary functions on a grid rather
L25@P0: than binary-valued ones (i. e., real-valued images rather than binary images). There is a simple intuition
L26@P0: underlying this generalization. Binary images are often used to specify the locations of certain features in
L27@P0: a picture. Rather than using a binary array to specify the presence or absence of a feature at each pixel, it

L67@P1: Efficient algorithms for computing the distance transform of a binary image using the L1 and L∞
L68@P1: distances were developed by Rosenfeld and Pfaltz [27]. Similar methods described in [5] have been
L69@P1: widely used to compute approximations to the EDT of a binary image. These algorithms can be easily

L71@P1: the L1 distance.
L72@P1: Our main result is a new linear-time algorithm for computing the distance transform of a sampled
L73@P1: function when distance is measured by the squared Euclidean distance. This in turn provides a new
L74@P1: technique for computing the exact EDT of a binary image, by computing the transform of the corresponding indicator function and taking square roots of the result. There are a number of other algorithms
L75@P1: for computing the EDT of a binary image in linear-time (e. g., [18, 7, 17]); however these methods are
L76@P1: quite involved and are not widely used in practice. In contrast, our algorithm is relatively simple, easy to

L80@P2: A sampled function is equivalent to a real-valued image. We use the terminology “distance transform
L81@P2: of a sampled function” for two reasons. First, we want to stress that the input is generally some kind of
L82@P2: cost function that is being transformed so as to incorporate spatial (or distance) information. Second,
L83@P2: there are methods for computing transforms of real-valued images based on minimum distances along
L84@P2: paths, where the cost of a path is the sum of values along the path [28]. We want to avoid confusion with
L85@P2: these methods which compute something quite different from what we consider here.
L86@P2: 1.1 Minimum convolution
L87@P2: The distance transform of a function is closely related to the min-convolution operation. This operation
L88@P2: and its continuous counterpart play an important role in grayscale morphology [21]. The min-convolution
L89@P2: of two functions f and g is defined as,
L90@P2: (f ⊗g)(p) = min

L96@P2: Just like standard convolution, this operation is commutative and associative,
L97@P2: f ⊗g = g⊗ f,
L98@P2: (f ⊗h)⊗g = f ⊗(h⊗g).
L99@P2: When d(p,q) = g(p−q), the distance transform of f under the distance d is the min-convolution
L100@P2: of f and g. The algorithms we describe in this paper can be seen as a algorithms for computing minconvolutions with restricted functions g. Our basic algorithms solve one-dimensional problems. The
L101@P2: multi-dimensional case is handled by decomposing it into a sequence of one-dimensional problems.
L102@P2: In the case of the squared Euclidean distance we are computing the min-convolution of a onedimensional function f and a parabola. We solve the problem by noting a relationship to lower envelopes
L103@P2: of parabolas. Lower envelopes of n parabolas can be computed in O(nlogn) time using the method in [8].
L104@P2: That method operates by sorting the parabolas in an appropriate order to be inserted in the lower envelope
L105@P2: in amortized constant time. In our case we get an O(n) algorithm because the parabolas have the same
L106@P2: shape and are already sorted in an appropriate order. Here n is the size of the domain of f . In the case of
L107@P2: the L1 distance we compute the min-convolution of a one-dimensional function f and a cone using the
L108@P2: classical approach of Rosenfeld and Pfaltz [27].
L109@P2: When d is the squared Euclidean and L1 distance, the corresponding g is convex. As described by
L110@P2: Eppstein [9] the problem of computing one-dimensional min-convolutions between arbitrary functions f
L111@P2: and convex functions g can be solved in O(n) time using the totally monotone matrix search algorithm
L112@P2: of [1]. When g is concave the problem can be solved in O(nα(n)) time using the matrix search algorithm
L113@P2: of [20], where α is the extremely slowly growing inverse Ackermann function.
L114@P2: Our algorithm for one-dimensional min-convolution with a parabola generalizes to computing the
L115@P2: min-convolution of an arbitrary one-dimensional function f and a convex or concave function g. If an
L116@P2: intersection point between shifted copies of g can be computed in constant time we get an O(n) method
L117@P2: for computing the min-convolution (the resulting algorithm is simpler than the linear-time method based
L118@P2: on matrix search, and also applies to the case when g is concave). Otherwise binary search can be used to
L119@P2: find an intersection in O(logn) time, yielding an O(nlogn) min-convolution algorithm.

L147@P3: 1.3 Classical EDT
L148@P3: An important consequence of our results is a new linear-time algorithm for computing the classical
L149@P3: Euclidean distance transform of a binary image. The method works by decomposing the problem into a
L150@P3: sequence of one-dimensional problems. This decomposition relies on the solution of the more general
L151@P3: problem, involving transforms of sampled functions. Thus, by solving a more general problem for the
L152@P3: one-dimensional case we obtain a simple algorithm for the multi-dimensional EDT.
L153@P3: While other methods for computing the EDT of binary functions existed before, these methods have
L154@P3: not been used in practice due to their practical complexity. In contrast, our algorithm has been used in a
L155@P3: wide variety of applications. For example, it was applied to study urban change in [15], motion planning
L156@P3: in [25], object recognition in [29] and image analysis PDEs in [22]. This illustrates the significance of
L157@P3: developing algorithms that are not only asymptotically optimal, but are also easy to implement and have
L158@P3: low complexity in practice.
